passages.t: Holy chambers and the wall of separation
passages.happening:
The man led Ezekiel to the outer court on the north, to blocks of chambers facing the temple courtyard, on three levels, and then to matching chambers on the south (verses 1-12). ‘The north and south chambers facing the temple courtyard are the holy chambers where the priests who approach the LORD will eat the most holy offerings’ (verse 13). When the priests leave the holy area, they must leave there the garments in which they serve and put on other clothes before going to the people (verse 14).

Then he measured the whole area on all four sides. ‘It had a wall all around, five hundred cubits long and five hundred cubits wide, to separate the holy from the common’ (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Israel's priests lived under rules about holy food and holy clothing. Portions of certain offerings were most holy and had to be eaten by the priests in a holy place, and Ezekiel's chambers provide it. On the Day of Atonement the high priest took off his linen garments before going out; Ezekiel extends that rule to all priests.

The logic is contagion. In priestly thought holiness, like uncleanness, could pass by contact, and the boundary protected both the holy things and the people. The square is large, about 260 meters on each side using the long cubit. The Hebrew of verses 16 to 19 reads rods, which would make it six times larger, but most translations, following the Greek and the parallel in 45:2, read cubits, as the BSB does.
passages.later: The priests were told, ‘You must distinguish between the holy and the common’ (Leviticus 10:10). The high priest removed his linen garments after the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:23).
passages.asks: The wall separated the holy from the common. Ask what in your life is set apart for God alone. And ask whether you have let the common crowd it out.
